This article applies `isoformic` to a complete public dataset.
It contains bulk RNA-seq of the anterodorsal bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (adBNST) of male mice.
The mice had six weeks of chronic variable mild stress and are compared with unstressed controls
[@degroat2024; BioProject [PRJNA984605](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/PRJNA984605)].
It shows a common outcome of transcript-level analysis.
Stress leaves the expression of genes almost unchanged, but changes which of their isoforms are expressed.

## The data

The 19 male samples (10 control, 9 stressed) were quantified with Salmon [@salmon]
against the GENCODE vM39 transcripts [@gencode].
The GRCm39 genome served as decoy, and each sample has 30 Gibbs draws.
Transcripts were tested with `swish` [@swish] on the inferential replicates.
Genes were tested with `DESeq2` on the summed counts.
The scripts that download the reads from SRA and run every step are in `data-raw/case_studies/` of the package repository.

The result is an `IsoformicExperiment` saved with `write_isoformic()`.
It keeps the complete differential expression tables (every tested transcript and gene).
The expression assays and exon structures cover only a panel of 47 genes, so that the object fits in the repository.
It is not installed with the package.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(isoformic)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

data_dir <- "data/mouse_bnst"
iso <- read_isoformic(data_dir)
iso
col_data(iso)
```

## Checking the samples first

A principal component analysis of the gene-level counts shows that the first component does not separate
the conditions.
It separates two groups of samples, one per range of SRA run accessions.
The groups are not annotated in GEO but are most likely two processing batches.
They are balanced between conditions (4 + 4 and 6 + 5 samples), so the tests can adjust for them.
`swish` stratifies its permutations by batch and `DESeq2` uses the design `~ batch + condition`.
Without the adjustment, no transcript and no gene reaches a false discovery rate of 5%,
and only 4 transcripts and no gene reach 10%.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
pca <- read_parquet(fs::path(data_dir, "sample_pca.parquet")) |>
  left_join(col_data(iso), by = "sample_id")
ggplot(pca, aes(PC1, PC2, color = batch, shape = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    x = sprintf("PC1 (%.0f%%)", 100 * pca$var_PC1[1]),
    y = sprintf("PC2 (%.0f%%)", 100 * pca$var_PC2[1])
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The sample far below the others on the second component (`control_3`) has the smallest library
(18.6 million read pairs) and the lowest mapping rate (72%).
It is kept in the analysis.
It is the first sample to check when a result depends on a single animal.

## Genes barely change, isoforms do

```{r}
iso@metadata[c("transcript_de", "gene_de")]
deg <- de_gene(iso)
det <- de_tx(iso)
c(
  genes_tested = nrow(deg),
  genes_fdr_5 = sum(deg$qvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
  transcripts_tested = nrow(det),
  transcripts_fdr_5 = sum(det$qvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
)
```

At a false discovery rate of 5%, `DESeq2` finds 4 genes and `swish` 126 transcripts.
Many of the transcript changes are moderate: 74 of the 126 transcripts change less than 2-fold.
This article therefore lowers the fold-change cutoff of the significance calls from the default of 1 to 0.5
(a 1.4-fold change):

```{r}
de_cutoffs(iso) <- list(log2fc = 0.5, pvalue = 0.05, use_fdr = TRUE)
```

The significant transcripts are not only protein coding isoforms.
More than half of them (69 of 126) are nonsense-mediated decay, retained intron or other non-coding isoforms
of protein coding genes, lncRNAs or a TEC transcript.

```{r}
det |>
  filter(qvalue < 0.05) |>
  left_join(tx_annot(iso), by = "transcript_id") |>
  count(transcript_type, sort = TRUE)
```

`isoform_switches()` relates the two levels.
With these cutoffs, 107 genes have one significant isoform each,
and none of them has a significant change of its total expression (`det_not_deg`).
A gene-level analysis would miss all of them.

```{r}
switches <- isoform_switches(iso)
table(switches$switch_type)
switches |>
  select(gene_name, n_det_up, n_det_down, det_sig_types, gene_log2FC, switch_type) |>
  head(10)
```

## A change of isoforms in *Celf1*

*Celf1* encodes an RNA-binding protein of the CELF family that regulates alternative splicing.
Its total expression does not change.
Its protein coding isoform `Celf1-203` goes up (log2 fold change 2.8),
from 1.2 to 13 transcripts per million on average.
`Celf1-203` encodes the same protein as `Celf1-205`, one of the two most expressed isoforms in the controls,
but starts at a first exon far upstream and has a longer last exon.
`Celf1-205` goes down from 16 to 11 transcripts per million, which is not significant on its own (q = 0.15).

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
plot_log2fc(iso, feature = "Celf1")
```

The expression profile shows the change in transcripts per million:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
plot_tx_expr(iso, gene_name = "Celf1", group = "condition")
```

and the genomic context shows the structures of the isoforms, with the differentially expressed ones outlined:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
plot_genomic_context(iso, gene_name = "Celf1")
```

## More genes with isoform-level changes

Most other panel genes (34 of the other 46) show the same pattern: a single significant isoform in a gene
whose total expression does not change significantly.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 10
plot_log2fc(iso, feature = c("Clstn2", "Gng7", "Npas2", "Ptk2b"), ncol = 2)
```

Some genes do not reach a false discovery rate of 5% once the batches are taken into account.
These include the genes of the first `isoformic` analysis of this dataset (*Trip12*, *Meg3* and *Map4*).
They also include classic stress response genes such as *Fkbp5* and *Sgk1*:

```{r}
det |>
  left_join(tx_annot(iso), by = "transcript_id") |>
  filter(gene_name %in% c("Trip12", "Meg3", "Map4", "Fkbp5", "Sgk1")) |>
  summarise(best_qvalue = min(qvalue), .by = gene_name)
```

## Enrichment by transcript type

The package directory holds the mouse Reactome pathways of MSigDB [@msigdb]
restricted to those with 15 to 500 tested genes.
`run_enrichment()` ranks the transcripts by fold change
and runs the enrichment separately for the protein coding isoforms and for the unproductive ones.

```{r}
#| warning: false
genesets <- read_gmt(fs::path(data_dir, "genesets.gmt"))
set.seed(42)
enrichment <- run_enrichment(iso, genesets, pval_cutoff = 0.05)
table(enrichment$experiment)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 10
plot_enrichment(
  enrichment,
  n = 25,
  experiments = c("protein_coding", "unproductive"),
  nes_cutoff = 1.5
)
```

Translation and mitochondrial pathways go down in the protein coding isoforms of the stressed animals
(translation and eukaryotic translation initiation, rRNA processing, mitochondrial translation,
aerobic respiration and respiratory electron transport, and complex IV assembly;
false discovery rate below 5%).
Complex I biogenesis, in the figure, goes down too, but not at a 5% false discovery rate.
Few pathways go up in the protein coding isoforms, and none of them is synaptic.
The ribosomal protein genes dominate the *nonsense-mediated decay* pathways of Reactome
(75 of the 92 leading-edge genes in the protein coding isoforms),
which is why those pathways are the most significant ones.
That pathway name describes the genes, not the transcript type.
In the unproductive isoforms the nonsense-mediated decay pathways and mitochondrial translation go down as well,
while apoptosis and programmed cell death go up.
